title: Phospholipids & Sphingolipids Metabolism
objectives: Understand the structure and classification of phospholipids and sphingolipids
Describe the biosynthetic pathways of major glycerophospholipids and sphingolipids
Explain the roles of these lipids in membrane structure and cell signaling
Analyze the catabolic pathways and associated lysosomal storage disorders
Identify clinical implications of phospholipid/sphingolipid metabolism

overview.title: Membrane Lipid Fundamentals
overview.content:
Phospholipids and sphingolipids are amphipathic lipids that form the structural basis of cellular membranes and function as signaling molecules. Phospholipids contain a glycerol backbone, while sphingolipids are built on sphingosine. Together they constitute ~50-60% of membrane lipids by mass.

Key Characteristics

FeaturePhospholipidsSphingolipids
BackboneGlycerol-3-phosphateSphingosine (18C amino alcohol)
Major ClassesPC, PE, PS, PI, PG, cardiolipinCeramides, sphingomyelins, glycosphingolipids
ChargeNeutral or anionicNeutral (except gangliosides)
FunctionsMembrane structure, signaling precursorsMembrane domains, cell recognition, signaling

phospholipid_metabolism.title: Glycerophospholipid Synthesis
phospholipid_metabolism.content:
Kennedy Pathway (de novo)

Location: ER membrane (cytosolic leaflet)

Key Enzymes: Choline/ethanolamine phosphotransferases

  1. Glycerol-3-P → Lysophosphatidic acid (GPAT)
  2. → Phosphatidic acid (AGPAT)
  3. → DAG (phosphatase) or CDP-DAG
  4. + Polar headgroup → PC/PE/PS/PI

Remodeling (Lands Cycle)

Process: Acyl chain exchange via PLA2 and LPCAT

Significance: Generates asymmetric membrane composition

Special Phospholipids

  • Cardiolipin: Mitochondrial inner membrane (4 acyl chains)
  • Plasmalogens: Ether lipids with vinyl ether bond (brain, heart)

sphingolipid_metabolism.title: Sphingolipid Biosynthesis
sphingolipid_metabolism.content:
de novo Pathway

Location: ER (steps 1-3), Golgi (modifications)

  1. Serine + Palmitoyl-CoA → 3-ketosphinganine (SPT, PLP-dependent)
  2. → Sphinganine (reductase)
  3. → Ceramide (acyl-CoA + DES1/2)
  4. → Sphingomyelin or glycosphingolipids

Complex Sphingolipids

  • Cerebrosides: Ceramide + single sugar (Glc/Gal)
  • Gangliosides: Sialic acid-containing (GM1, GM2)
  • Globosides: Multiple neutral sugars (Gb3 in Fabry)

Regulation

Control Points: SPT (vitamin B6), ceramide synthases (CERS1-6)

Sphingosine-1-P: Signaling metabolite (S1P receptors)

degradation.title: Degradation Pathways
degradation.content:
Phospholipid Catabolism

  • Phospholipases: PLA1, PLA2, PLC, PLD cleave specific bonds
  • Ether Lipid Breakdown: Peroxisomal α-oxidation

Sphingolipid Catabolism

  • Lysosomal Enzymes: Sequential sugar removal (exohydrolases)
  • Ceramidases: Generate sphingosine for recycling
  • Defects: Cause lysosomal storage disorders

Membrane Asymmetry

  • Flippases: ATP-dependent translocation (P4-ATPases)
  • Scramblases: Calcium-activated bidirectional movement
  • PS Exposure: Apoptotic signal (annexin V binding)

clinical_correlations.title: Clinical Correlations
clinical_correlations.content:
Phospholipid Disorders

  • ARDS: Surfactant deficiency (dipalmitoyl-PC)
  • RCDP: Plasmalogen deficiency (peroxisomal disorder)
  • Antiphospholipid Syndrome: Autoantibodies to β2GPI-PS

Sphingolipidoses

  • Gaucher: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency (glucosylceramide)
  • Tay-Sachs: Hexosaminidase A (GM2 ganglioside)
  • Niemann-Pick: Sphingomyelinase (Type A/B) or NPC1 (Type C)

Therapeutics

  • Enzyme Replacement: Imiglucerase (Gaucher)
  • Substrate Reduction: Miglustat (glucosylceramide synthase)
  • S1P Modulators: Fingolimod (MS treatment)

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
Why do phospholipids spontaneously form bilayers?+
Their amphipathic nature creates hydrophobic effects that drive tail aggregation while polar headgroups interact with aqueous environments, making bilayers the lowest free energy configuration.
How does vitamin B6 deficiency affect sphingolipids?+
PLP is a cofactor for serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT), so deficiency impairs de novo sphingolipid synthesis, particularly impacting myelination.
What distinguishes lipid rafts from other membrane domains?+
Rrafts are sphingolipid/cholesterol-rich microdomains with packed acyl chains that concentrate signaling proteins, while non-raft regions are more fluid and phospholipid-rich.
Why do sphingolipid storage disorders primarily affect the nervous system?+
Neurons have high sphingolipid content in membranes (especially gangliosides) and limited regenerative capacity, making them vulnerable to lysosomal accumulation.
